Getting started with tidystata

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

Did participants enjoy the community course? How did their assessment scores compare across centres? tidystata helps answer these first questions inside a tidyverse workflow: start with a tibble, inspect it, prepare columns with mutate(), and pass results to the next step with |>.

Install tidystata using the instructions on the package homepage. We attach dplyr and tibble individually; the full tidyverse package is not required.

Meet the survey

Twelve participants attended courses at Riverside and Hilltop. Each answered a yes/no satisfaction question and two assessment items. Some answers are missing, and income arrived as text.

library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(tidystata)

survey <- tribble(
  ~id, ~centre,     ~satisfied, ~income_text, ~score1, ~score2,
    1, "Riverside", "Yes",     "1,200",           2,       4,
    2, "Riverside", "Yes",     "1,500",           4,      NA,
    3, "Riverside", "No",      "",               NA,      NA,
    4, "Riverside", NA,        "-99",             6,       8,
    5, "Riverside", "Yes",     "2,200",           8,      10,
    6, "Riverside", "Yes",     "1,800",           4,       6,
    7, "Hilltop",   "No",      "1,400",           3,       5,
    8, "Hilltop",   "Yes",     "2,100",           5,       7,
    9, "Hilltop",   "No",      "2,600",           7,       9,
   10, "Hilltop",   "Yes",     NA,                9,      NA,
   11, "Hilltop",   "Yes",     "2,300",          NA,       8,
   12, "Hilltop",   NA,        "1,700",           6,       8
)

survey |> codebook()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   variable    type          n unique
#>   <chr>       <chr>     <int>  <int>
#> 1 id          double       12     12
#> 2 centre      character    12      2
#> 3 satisfied   character    10      2
#> 4 income_text character    11     11
#> 5 score1      double       10      8
#> 6 score2      double        9      7

There are six participants per centre. The codebook shows which columns contain text, how many values are observed, and where the gaps are. An identifier is numeric too, but we will select assessment items deliberately when summarising.

Prepare measurements with mutate()

The survey form uses -99 for an undisclosed income. Read the numeric text, turn that code into NA, and calculate an average across the two assessment items.

prepared <- survey |>
  mutate(
    income = destring(income_text) |> mvdecode(-99),
    score = row_mean(pick(score1, score2)),
    answered = row_non_miss(pick(score1, score2))
  )

prepared |> select(id, income, score, answered)
#> # A tibble: 12 × 4
#>       id income score answered
#>    <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>    <int>
#>  1     1   1200     3        2
#>  2     2   1500     4        1
#>  3     3     NA    NA        0
#>  4     4     NA     7        2
#>  5     5   2200     9        2
#>  6     6   1800     5        2
#>  7     7   1400     4        2
#>  8     8   2100     6        2
#>  9     9   2600     8        2
#> 10    10     NA     9        1
#> 11    11   2300     8        1
#> 12    12   1700     7        2

Participant 2 has one assessment answer, so the average uses that answer. Participant 3 has none: the average is NA and answered is zero. destring() also reads the thousands separators; blank text becomes missing.

Count responses

How many participants were satisfied?

prepared |> tab(satisfied)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   satisfied     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
#>   <chr>     <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 No            3    25    25      30        30
#> 2 Yes           7    58.3  83.3    70       100
#> 3 NA            2    16.7 100      NA        NA

Seven said yes. That is 58.3% of all twelve participants, or 70% of the ten who answered. The percent and valid columns make both denominators visible. The two missing answers remain a category.

Results are tibbles here, so ordinary dplyr verbs can answer a follow-up question:

prepared |>
  tab(satisfied, .by = centre) |>
  filter(satisfied == "Yes") |>
  select(centre, n, valid)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   centre        n valid
#>   <chr>     <int> <dbl>
#> 1 Hilltop       3    60
#> 2 Riverside     4    80

Compare measurements

Now compare the assessment average across centres.

prepared |>
  summ(score, .by = centre, .stat = c("n", "mean", "sd"))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   centre    type      n  mean    sd
#>   <chr>     <chr> <int> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Hilltop   dbl       6   7    1.79
#> 2 Riverside dbl       5   5.6  2.41

Each mean uses the observed scores in that centre. The returned table is ready for another pipeline; no results need to be copied out of console output. Use tabstat() when a compact table of means is enough.
